bibl.title: The sensory nature of mnemonic representation in the primate prefrontal cortex

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: Our results indicated that during the delay period when sensory information was no longer available, neuronal discharge was modulated by the luminance of the stimulus appearing in the receptive field, and was directly correlated with psychophysical performance in the task.

span.label: delay-period activity in primate prefrontal cortex during visual working memory
span.quote: The primate prefrontal cortex (PFC) is a critical node of the network that mediates working memory, one component of which is the ability to retain and mentally manipulate a stimulus over the time scale of seconds1,2.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: To explore the relationship between neuronal activity and behavioral performance, we recorded from the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex of monkeys trained to perform a delayed discrimination task.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Dorsolateral PFC runs two superimposed processes - a slowly decaying sensory representation plus a response-preparation signal that ramps toward the saccade - whose sum produces the observed delay activity
span.quote: Based on these considerations, we propose that dorsolateral PFC encompasses neurons engaged in at least two separate processes: a sensory representation that remains fairly constant or slowly decays during the delay period, and a response preparation that increases toward the onset of the saccade (Fig. 8).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The motor plan emerges from a network of neurons that keep holding sensory information, rather than from a discrete sensory-to-motor transformation stage in single neurons
span.quote: Our present findings favor the view that a motor plan is an emergent property of a network composed in part by neurons sustaining sensory information, rather than involving a discrete decision stage in which sensory parameters are transformed into motor variables by single neurons

span.label: The task never required luminance itself to be remembered, only the relative comparison
span.quote: Our task did not explicitly require the animals to remember the luminance of the stimuli; the subject needed only to discriminate between their relative difference.

span.label: Not all recorded neurons fitted the sensory account; some reflected only the motor response
span.quote: This was representative of our population, although we did observe some neurons, particularly those with strong pre-saccadic responses, that only reflected the animal’s motor response.

span.label: The two results on the same measure hold under opposite spatial conditions.
span.quote: Delay period activity was not significantly modulated by the presence of a distractor outside the receptive field, when the target appeared inside (Fig. 4a; regression analysis, p > 0.3). However, delay period activity was significantly dependent on contrast ratio when the distractor appeared in the receptive field

span.label: The inference the whole result rests on is reported by the authors as contested.
span.quote: Although neurons in the primate prefrontal cortex discharge while a stimulus is maintained in memory, it has been argued that temporal correlation does not necessarily imply involvement of this activity in perceptual memory

span.label: The analysis population was chosen by an explicit decision not to exclude two neuron types.
span.quote: We based the analysis of our results on the entire sample, rather than ignore the contribution of primarily cue and saccade neurons to the delay period activity

span.label: eye-movement parameters as the cause of the contrast-ratio effect
span.quote: To ensure that this effect was not due to eye-movement parameters, we repeated our analysis after including saccade metrics in the regression model

span.label: delay period activity
span.quote: Delay period activity was not significantly modulated by the presence of a distractor outside the receptive field, when the target appeared inside (Fig. 4a; regression analysis, p > 0.3). However, delay period activity was significantly dependent on contrast ratio when the distractor appeared in the receptive field

span.label: distractor
span.quote: Delay period activity was not significantly modulated by the presence of a distractor outside the receptive field, when the target appeared inside (Fig. 4a; regression analysis, p > 0.3). However, delay period activity was significantly dependent on contrast ratio when the distractor appeared in the receptive field

span.label: contrast ratio
span.quote: Delay period activity was not significantly modulated by the presence of a distractor outside the receptive field, when the target appeared inside (Fig. 4a; regression analysis, p > 0.3). However, delay period activity was significantly dependent on contrast ratio when the distractor appeared in the receptive field

span.label: receptive field
span.quote: Delay period activity was not significantly modulated by the presence of a distractor outside the receptive field, when the target appeared inside (Fig. 4a; regression analysis, p > 0.3). However, delay period activity was significantly dependent on contrast ratio when the distractor appeared in the receptive field

span.label: perceptual memory
span.quote: Although neurons in the primate prefrontal cortex discharge while a stimulus is maintained in memory, it has been argued that temporal correlation does not necessarily imply involvement of this activity in perceptual memory

span.label: delay period activity - MODULATED OR NOT DEPENDING ON WHERE THE STIMULI WERE: not significantly modulated by a distractor outside the receptive field while the target was inside, and significantly dependent on contrast ratio when the distractor was inside it; the same measure yields a null and a positive result, and only the spatial condition separates them
span.quote: Delay period activity was not significantly modulated by the presence of a distractor outside the receptive field, when the target appeared inside (Fig. 4a; regression analysis, p > 0.3). However, delay period activity was significantly dependent on contrast ratio when the distractor appeared in the receptive field

span.label: delay activity as memory - AN INFERENCE THE PAPER REPORTS AS DISPUTED: neurons discharge while a stimulus is held in memory, and it has been argued that temporal correlation does not necessarily imply involvement of that activity in perceptual memory, so the field's central inference is named as contested inside a paper that relies on it
span.quote: Although neurons in the primate prefrontal cortex discharge while a stimulus is maintained in memory, it has been argued that temporal correlation does not necessarily imply involvement of this activity in perceptual memory

span.label: the analysed sample - THE WHOLE RECORDING, BY DECISION: rather than dropping neurons whose responses were mainly to the cue or the saccade, the authors state they used the entire sample so as not to ignore those neurons' contribution to delay period activity
span.quote: We based the analysis of our results on the entire sample, rather than ignore the contribution of primarily cue and saccade neurons to the delay period activity

span.label: contradicts → previous studies of delay-period activity in a discrimination task concluding that responses reflect the outcome of a perceptual decision (the paper's refs 18,19)
span.quote: In contrast to these results, previous studies analyzing activity in the delay period of a discrimination task concluded that neuronal responses best correlate with the outcome of a perceptual decision18,19.

span.label: builds-on → previous dorsolateral prefrontal experiments using the anti-saccade paradigm, spatial match-to-sample and conditional response tasks (the paper's refs 10,28,29)
span.quote: The present findings are in agreement with previous experiments in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex suggesting that neuronal activity in a mnemonic task represents the remembered visual stimulus, as demonstrated by the anti-saccade paradigm, spatial match-to-sample and conditional response tasks10,28,29.

span.label: distractor —causes→ delay period activity
span.note: holds when: when the distractor is outside the receptive field and the target inside it · direction on the measure: no-change
span.quote: Delay period activity was not significantly modulated by the presence of a distractor outside the receptive field, when the target appeared inside (Fig. 4a; regression analysis, p > 0.3). However, delay period activity was significantly dependent on contrast ratio when the distractor appeared in the receptive field

span.label: contrast ratio —causes→ delay period activity
span.note: holds when: when the distractor appeared in the receptive field
span.quote: Delay period activity was not significantly modulated by the presence of a distractor outside the receptive field, when the target appeared inside (Fig. 4a; regression analysis, p > 0.3). However, delay period activity was significantly dependent on contrast ratio when the distractor appeared in the receptive field

span.label: t-test
span.quote: First, their firing had to be significantly elevated from baseline fixation for at least one task epoch (paired t-test, p < 0.05).

span.label: regression
span.quote: We tested the effect of stimulus luminance on neuronal responses by performing a regression analysis (Fig. 4).

span.label: linear regression
span.quote: We determined the effect of contrast ratio on neuronal firing rate by performing a linear regression using the following model.

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: The interaction between time and contrast was not significant (two-way ANOVA, F66,4284 = 0.57, p > 0.9), although the ANOVA test confirmed that the main effects of both contrast and time were significant

span.label: ROC analysis
span.quote: We used receiver-operating characteristic (ROC) analysis48 to determine the ability of each neuron to distinguish between a target and a distractor placed in its receptive field.

span.label: coefficient of determination
span.quote: We selected a range of stimulus luminance over which performance varied in an essentially linear fashion when plotted against the logarithm of the contrast ratio (linear regression, R2 = 0.99, 0.97 for the two animals respecnature

span.label: p-value
span.quote: However, delay period activity was significantly dependent on contrast ratio when the distractor appeared in the receptive field (regression analysis, p < 10–5).

span.label: Delay-period firing of prefrontal neurons was graded by the luminance of the stimulus in the receptive field, i.e. by its sensory attributes rather than by the animal's choice.
span.quote: However, delay period activity was significantly dependent on contrast ratio when the distractor appeared in the receptive field (regression analysis, p < 10–5).

span.label: The luminance modulation of delay activity survived control for saccade metrics, showing it was not an artefact of the motor response.
span.quote: significant (p < 10–5), indicating that the modulation was independent of the motor response.

span.label: Mnemonic prefrontal activity was directly correlated with the monkeys' psychophysical performance.
span.quote: Activity of neurons in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex during the delay period of a mnemonic task was modulated by the perceived sensory attributes of remembered stimuli, and correlated directly with psychophysical performance in the task.

span.label: Neuronal discriminability between target and distractor tracked contrast ratio across the entire delay, not only early in it.
span.quote: Our results indicated that the ability to discriminate between a target and distractor was dependent on the contrast ratio throughout the delay period (Fig. 5).

span.label: The graded delay responses contradict the prediction of a pure decision-formation account, which requires responses to converge once sensory evidence has been accumulated.
span.quote: Contrary to that prediction, our results indicated a graded pattern of responses related to luminance throughout the delay.

span.label: A large minority of neurons kept firing above baseline for a distractor in the receptive field even when the saccade was made away from it.
span.quote: The effect was statistically significant for 42% of the neurons (45% and 25% for the two animals respectively; t-test, p < 0.05).

span.label: The contrast effect replicated when the delay length varied unpredictably, ruling out the possibility that it depended on a fixed, predictable delay allowing early motor planning.
span.quote: The effect of stimulus contrast across the population was statistically significant when the distractor appeared inside the receptive field (two-way ANOVA, p < 10–5) but not significant when the target appeared in the receptive field (p > 0.3) as was the case when using a fixed delay interval (Fig. 7).

span.label: Reward expectation cannot explain the pattern, because firing was strongest in the condition of minimum expected reward.
span.quote: Indeed, neurons discharged more vigorously when the distractor appearing in their receptive field was identical to the target, the condition that represented the minimum reward expectation (Fig. 4b).

span.label: area under the ROC curve
span.quote: The area under the ROC curve represents the probability that of a given pair of responses, one belonging to a target and one to a distractor, the target will evoke the higher discharge rate.

span.label: short-term memory trace for an unattended stimulus
span.term: short-term memory trace for an unattended stimulus
span.quote: In this context, delay-period responses to a distractor can be thought of as short-term memory traces for an unattended stimulus.

span.label: working memory
span.quote: working memory, one component of which is the ability to retain and mentally manipulate a stimulus over the time scale of seconds

span.label: luminance / contrast ratio of the distractor relative to the target
span.term: luminance / contrast ratio of the distractor relative to the target
span.quote: The luminance of one stimulus (target) remained fixed in all trials, whereas the luminance of the second stimulus (distractor) varied between the background and the luminance of the target.

span.label: stimulus position relative to the neuron's receptive field (inside vs outside)
span.term: stimulus position relative to the neuron's receptive field (inside vs outside)
span.quote: which could appear inside or outside the neuron’s receptive field

span.label: delay duration (fixed 3 s vs randomly varying 0.15-3 s)
span.term: delay duration (fixed 3 s vs randomly varying 0.15-3 s)
span.quote: To test this hypothesis, we recorded activity from 24 additional neurons, tested with a delay period that could vary between 0.15 and 3 s in each trial.

span.label: neuronal firing rate in the cue, delay and saccade epochs
span.term: neuronal firing rate in the cue, delay and saccade epochs
span.quote: Firing rate was calculated in three epochs: cue (0.5 s), delay (3 s following the offset of the cue) and saccade (0.25 s following the offset of the fixation point).

span.label: percentage of correct saccades (psychophysical performance)
span.quote: The animals’ percentage of correct responses depended on the contrast ratio of the two stimuli (Fig. 1c and d).

span.label: saccade metrics (latency, amplitude, accuracy, maximal speed, duration)
span.term: saccade metrics (latency, amplitude, accuracy, maximal speed, duration)
span.quote: To ensure that any effect of luminance was not accounted for simply by variations in saccadic eye movements, we repeated the regression analysis including five descriptors of the saccade metrics in the model: latency, amplitude, accuracy, maximal speed and duration.

span.label: 52 — isolated prefrontal neurons analysed in the fixed-delay experiment, from two rhesus monkeys
span.quote: We analyzed activity from 52 isolated neurons in the prefrontal cortex (areas 8 and 46) of two rhesus monkeys (Fig. 1a).

span.label: 75% — behavioural accuracy threshold, reached at a distractor/target contrast ratio of 1-4%
span.quote: They achieved 75% correct responses when the contrast ratio of the distractor relative to the target was 1 to 4%.

span.label: 42% — proportion of neurons with significantly elevated delay activity for a distractor in the receptive field
span.quote: The effect was statistically significant for 42% of the neurons (45% and 25% for the two animals respectively; t-test, p < 0.05).

span.label: 24 — additional neurons recorded in the variable-delay control experiment
span.quote: To test this hypothesis, we recorded activity from 24 additional neurons, tested with a delay period that could vary between 0.15 and 3 s in each trial.

span.label: –0.037, p < 10–5 — regression slope of normalized delay firing on log contrast ratio when the distractor was in the receptive field
span.quote: The regression slope was significantly different from zero (–0.037, p < 10–5).

span.label: R2 = 0.99, 0.97 — fit of psychophysical performance to the logarithm of contrast ratio for the two monkeys
span.quote: We selected a range of stimulus luminance over which performance varied in an essentially linear fashion when plotted against the logarithm of the contrast ratio (linear regression, R2 = 0.99, 0.97 for the two animals respecnature

span.label: F66,4284 = 0.57, p > 0.9 — non-significant time-by-contrast interaction in the ANOVA on ROC discrimination probability
span.quote: The interaction between time and contrast was not significant (two-way ANOVA, F66,4284 = 0.57, p > 0.9), although the ANOVA test confirmed that the main effects of both contrast and time were significant
